The e-Nothi initiative is designed to streamline documentation and workflows, reduce reliance on paper-based processes, and enhance operational efficiency through digitalization.
Commenting on the achievement, Rizwan Dawood Shams, managing director of IPDC Finance PLC., said: “We are honored to receive this recognition at the ADFIAP Development Awards 2026. It reflects our commitment to leveraging technology to make our operations more efficient, responsive and sustainable. e-Nothi is an important milestone in our digital transformation journey, and this achievement reflects the dedication of our team and the continued support of our partners and stakeholders.”
The Association of Development Financing Institutions in Asia and the Pacific (ADFIAP) organizes the ADFIAP Development Awards to recognize notable development initiatives and practices undertaken by its member institutions in areas such as technology, sustainability, corporate governance and social development.
The award underscores IPDC Finance’s continued commitment to digital innovation, process modernization and sustainable operational practices, reinforcing its focus on building a more efficient and technology-driven organization.

item.title: A roof is not enough
item.description:
A family finds a cheaper home on the outskirts of Dhaka. On paper, it looks affordable. But the father now spends hours commuting to work and a sizeable share of his income on transport. The children have little space to study. Waterlogging makes the neighborhood difficult to access during heavy rain. And every rent increase forces the family to reconsider what to cut from the monthly budget: food, healthcare, education, or savings.
So, is this really affordable housing?
This is the question we need to ask as we observe World Habitat Day and reflect on the call for “Adequate Housing for All.” Housing is too often discussed in terms of buildings: how many apartments have been constructed, how many plots have been developed, or how many families own their homes. But adequate housing is not simply four walls and a roof. It is about whether a home allows people to live safely, affordably, and with dignity and whether its location enables them to participate in the city.
For Bangladesh, this distinction is increasingly important. The 2022 Population and Housing Census shows that while about 80.8 percent of households nationally lived in their own dwellings, the figure was only 55.6 percent in urban areas. Around 34.7 percent of urban households were renters who did not own another dwelling elsewhere.
The more recent picture suggests that rental dependence remains significant. According to reporting based on Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics data, around 45 percent of households in Dhaka Division were renting or subletting their dwellings in 2023, compared with about 19 percent nationally. At the same time, the House Rent Index has continued to rise; BBS data show a 5.19 percent year-on-year increase in the July-September 2025 quarter, followed by 5.24 percent in October-December 2025.
These figures make the issue very tangible. For a large share of urban Bangladesh, housing is not an ownership question; it is a rental question. Homeownership therefore cannot be the only measure of housing success. For millions of Bangladeshis, particularly migrants, young workers, students, newly formed households, and low- and middle-income families, rental housing is not a temporary arrangement on the way to ownership. Rental housing is their housing.
Yet our housing discourse continues to focus heavily on land ownership, apartment ownership and new construction. Rental housing deserves far greater policy attention. We need better rental-market data, greater tenure security, transparent mechanisms for rent adjustment and incentives to expand affordable rental housing in well-connected locations.
This brings us to perhaps the most overlooked dimension of housing affordability: location.
A Tk10,000 home close to employment, public transport, schools and healthcare may ultimately be more affordable than a Tk7,000 home that requires several hours and substantial transport expenditure every day. Housing costs therefore cannot be understood separately from mobility costs. We need to start asking not simply, “How much does this house cost?” but, “How much does it cost this household to live here?”
Housing also has consequences that extend far beyond urban planning. Housing policy is education policy, health policy and, increasingly, climate policy. Consider a child living in an overcrowded home without adequate lighting, ventilation or a quiet place to study. Improving the school alone cannot remove all the disadvantages that child experiences. Housing conditions influence sleep, health, concentration and learning opportunities. Excessive rent can also leave families with less money for education, nutrition and healthcare.
Climate change adds another layer of urgency. In Bangladesh, flooding, waterlogging, cyclones, river erosion, salinity and extreme heat already affect where and how people live. A dwelling cannot be called adequate if it is affordable today but repeatedly flooded tomorrow, or if poor ventilation makes it dangerously uncomfortable during extreme heat.
Climate-resilient housing therefore requires more than stronger buildings. It requires risk-sensitive land-use planning, protection of wetlands and floodplains, better drainage, heat-sensitive design, energy efficiency, resilient infrastructure and community-based adaptation.
But resilience should not become an excuse for displacement. This is particularly relevant to informal settlements and historic neighborhoods such as Puran Dhaka. Demolishing older housing and replacing it with expensive apartments may improve physical building quality while making the neighborhood unaffordable to its original residents. The result can be better buildings but less inclusive cities.
Where feasible, upgrading existing communities should therefore come before displacement-oriented redevelopment. Better sanitation, drainage, water supply, waste management, public spaces, structural improvements and energy efficiency can improve housing conditions while allowing communities to retain their livelihoods, social networks and cultural identity. This principle is especially important in historic neighborhoods.
Bangladesh ultimately needs to move from counting houses to measuring housing adequacy. A national framework could assess affordability, tenure security, habitability, basic services, accessibility, location, climate resilience, and social and cultural adequacy. These dimensions could also be mapped through GIS to identify neighborhoods where different forms of housing deprivation overlap and where place-specific interventions are needed.
This would shift the housing conversation from “How many units have we built?” to a much more meaningful question: “Are people actually able to live well in those homes?”
World Habitat Day should therefore prompt us to ask a different question. Not simply: How many houses does Bangladesh need? We should ask: Can a family afford its home without sacrificing food, education or healthcare? Can a worker reach employment without losing hours every day? Can a child study safely at home? Can a tenant live without constant insecurity? Can an elderly person reach essential services? Can a community survive both climate risks and redevelopment pressures?
If the answer is no, providing a roof is not enough. For Bangladesh, “Adequate Housing for All” should not remain an annual slogan. It should become a principle that guides how we plan our cities, invest in infrastructure, regulate rental markets, respond to climate risks and measure development itself. Because the real success of housing policy will not ultimately be counted in apartments, plots or buildings. It will be measured by whether those homes allow people to live with security, dignity and opportunity.
Mowtushi Poit is Assistant Professor, Bangladesh Institute of Governance and Management (BIGM).

item.title: Our road safety and the ticket of poverty to endanger others without consequence
item.description:
Picture your own evening in Dhaka. You leave work tired and reach a busy crossing. Your child waits beside you, holding your hand. A battery powered rickshaw comes straight at you on the wrong side of the road.
It has no number plate. Its driver holds no licence. No fitness test has ever checked its brakes. You pull your child back, and it rushes past. You breathe out and cross, because there is no other way home.
The Bangladesh Road Transport Authority estimates that 10 to 12 lakh of these vehicles run in this city, though no office holds an exact count. Some evenings, someone does not pull back in time. The driver who hits them will most likely never face a conviction.
The scale is not a matter of opinion. Road accidents killed 9,111 people and injured 14,812 others across Bangladesh in 2025, a nearly six percent rise over the previous year. In Dhaka alone, 1,384 people were killed in road crashes between 2020 and July this year , and pedestrians, the people with no vehicle and no fault, made up 42.77 percent of the dead. Auto-rickshaws, CNG three-wheelers, and legunas together were involved in well over a tenth of all recorded crashes in that same stretch. These are abstractions. More so, they are people crossing a road that never had a working signal.
Ask anyone who commutes through Kuril, Mirpur, or Gulistan on a given evening, and battery rickshaws will come up before anything else does.
The Bangladesh Power Development Board estimates that 45 to 50 lakh battery powered rickshaws and easy bikes now operate nationwide , most outside any formal registry. Dhaka's new AI powered traffic camera system , launched this year to automatically fine violators, has run into exactly this wall.
Cameras can identify a bus or a car by its plate, but most auto-rickshaws carry no digital plate at all, so the system cannot see them. Drivers know it. Wrong way movement on routes such as 300 Feet Road, Kuril-Badda, and Moghbazar continues largely unpunished, because the tool built to catch it cannot legally identify the offender.
This is not a story of reckless individuals alone. It is a story of a vehicle class that grew faster than any ministry chose to regulate it, because regulating it would mean confronting the livelihoods of millions of low income drivers at once.
Even editorial voices now conceding the need for authorized manufacturing, registration, and defined routes warn against a blanket crackdown that would strip a poor driver of his only income overnight. Both things are true simultaneously.
That is precisely the trap.
Move from three-wheelers to buses and trucks and the same pattern holds.
A 2025 investigation found that 63.29 percent of people seeking BRTA services had to pay a bribe , and unskilled drivers routinely buy what insiders call a contract licence, a stamp of competence with no test behind it.
A driver earning a few thousand taka a month cannot afford the weeks a proper licensing process demands, so he pays the shortcut instead, and the owner who hires him never asks for a genuine result, because a cheap, undertrained driver saves the owner money either way.
Here poverty stops being an excuse and becomes a shield. Only about five percent of road accident cases in Bangladesh end in conviction . The maximum sentence for causing death through reckless driving once stood at seven years .
In 1985, after truckers protested, the Ershad government cut it to three, where it remains. Compensation follows the same script. The Road Transport Act 2018 quietly replaced a victim's right to sue an owner in court with a right to merely apply for aid from a state fund, and today only around five percent of victims ever receive a payout , capped at five lakh taka for a death regardless of fault.
Lawmakers assumed, correctly in most cases, that a driver or owner cannot afford a real settlement, so the state built a shared fund instead of individual liability, quietly telling every reckless driver that poverty, his own and his employer's, will absorb the cost of whoever he kills.
This pattern is not unique to us. Research on paratransit across the developing world finds the same feature everywhere, informal three-wheelers filling gaps formal transit leaves behind, operating with almost no oversight, and the resulting safety costs landing hardest on the poorest road users. What varies is how seriously a government decides to close that gap.
The people dying under these wheels are, overwhelmingly, just as poor as the men driving them.
This is poverty killing poverty, while transport owners' associations that resist digitized licensing and oppose stricter fitness checks sit comfortably above it all.
Real reform is not sympathy for reckless driving. It is mandatory digital plates and a real national registry for every battery rickshaw on the road, so an AI camera can finally see what it is built to catch.
It is an enforceable right to sue, so liability lands on the owner, not the driver he underpays. It is a compensation fund that pays out in weeks, not years, and scales with fault.
Until then, poverty will keep functioning exactly as it does now on our roads, not as a tragedy the state is fighting, but as a ticket the state has already priced in.
AKM Lutfur Rahman is a Commonwealth Scholar, Road Safety Expert, and experienced Transport Director having held high-impact positions at the British High Commission, CARE Bangladesh, and in roles affiliated with the US Embassy. Nafis Ehsas Chowdhury is Officer, Corporate HR & OD at Ha-Meem Group and an Independent Columnist.

item.title: Tangail eyes tourism boom with rich heritage and natural beauty
item.description:
Rich in history, cultural heritage, and natural beauty, Tangail has vast potential to develop as a major tourism destination, with its historic landmarks, forests, traditional handloom industry, and distinctive products offering a diverse experience for visitors.
The district is home to Mughal-era Atia Mosque, Mohera, Hemnagar, Karotia, Delduar, Pakutia, and Dhanbari zamindar mansions, Madhupur National Park, Pirgachha Rubber Garden, and Jamuna Bridge. Its proximity to Dhaka and relatively easy road connectivity further enhance its prospects as a tourism hub.
Tourism could also generate employment for local guides, resort operators, restaurants, and handicraft businesses while creating opportunities for increased local revenue through public-private investment.
Among the district's natural attractions, Madhupur National Park stands out for its extensive forest landscape and wildlife. Spread across more than 20,000 acres, the park offers visitors a break from urban life. It is also home to a deer breeding centre.
Pirgachha Rubber Garden in Madhupur is another popular destination. Visitors can enjoy the changing appearance of its large rubber trees across the seasons and, with permission, observe the process of collecting and processing raw rubber at a nearby factory.
Atia Mosque in Delduar is one of Tangail's notable historical landmarks. Built in a distinctive Mughal-Sultanate architectural style, the single-domed mosque was once featured on the Tk10 banknote. The 201-domed mosque in Gopalpur is another attraction, featuring eight tall minarets, four of which are 101 feet high.
The Jamuna Bridge area in Kalihati draws visitors for its river views, open air, and sunrise and sunset scenes. The nearby Jamuna Railway Bridge has also become an attraction.
Upendra Sarobar in Nagarpur, around 25km from Tangail town, is another scenic destination. The lake, locally known as “Baro Ghatla Dighi,” has 12 ghats and was excavated in 1341 Bengali calendar to address the area's drinking water shortage.
Tangail's cultural identity is further strengthened by Porabari Chamcham, a traditional sweet with a history of around two centuries, and its famous handloom sarees. Visitors can explore the district's historic zamindar mansions, particularly Mohera Zamindar Bari, one of the most popular heritage sites.
Local residents say the tourism sector needs better preservation of historical sites, quality hotels, and resorts, improved security, and stronger digital promotion to reach domestic and international tourists.
Tangail Deputy Commissioner Sharifa Haque said the district's 12 upazilas offered diverse natural and cultural attractions. “Tourism can play an important role in the local economy. We have to present Tangail's history, heritage, culture, and natural beauty to the world, and we are working towards that goal,” she said.
Local lawmaker and State Minister Sultan Salahuddin Tuku said plans were underway to develop Tangail as a modern tourism hub, including a mini tourism centre around the DC Lake and a larger tourism destination in the char areas.
He said improved connectivity, cleanliness, scenic development, and tourist facilities would be essential to unlock the district's tourism potential and create more employment opportunities.

item.title: Case filed over attack on journalists at RU
item.description:
A case was filed against unidentified people on Monday over an attack on journalists on the Rajshahi University (RU) campus allegedly by leaders and activists of Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD).
Md Munir Hossain, deputy registrar of Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Hall, filed the case with Motihar Police Station, said its Officer-in-Charge Golam Kabir.
“We have recorded a case. We have started working on it and will take action after investigation,” he said.
However, journalists covering the university expressed dissatisfaction over the decision to file the case against unidentified suspects.
They demanded that those involved in the attack be identified and arrested quickly and that the university administration take visible and effective action against them.
Ashiqul Islam Dhrubo, president of RU Press Club, said there was no ambiguity about the identities of those involved in the attack.
“We have all the footage of the attack, and people across the country have seen it. It is as clear as daylight who was involved. Their names, posts and identities have already been published in news reports,” he said.
“There is no question of filing a case against unidentified persons. We demand that the names of everyone involved be included in the case and that they be arrested as soon as possible,” Ashiqul added.
Former RU Journalists’ Association President Irfan Tamim also criticised the decision, describing it as extremely disappointing.
Ten people, including four journalists, were injured when JCD leaders and activists allegedly attacked them in front of Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Hall around 8:30pm on Sunday.
Several JCD leaders and activists, including university unit Vice-President Ahsan Habib, were alleged to have been involved in the attack.
The attack reportedly took place after journalists took photographs of locally made weapons allegedly displayed for an attack on a rival group.
The injured journalists include Arifuzzaman Qurban, RU correspondent of bdnews24.com; Zahidul Islam, correspondent of Agamir Somoy; Noor Ahsan Mridul, correspondent of The Daily Star; and Mainul Islam Raju, correspondent of Samakal.
Meanwhile, a five-member committee was formed to investigate the incident.

item.title: Without reconciliation, society remains deeply divided
item.description:
Justice for crimes is essential. At the same time, reconciliation is needed. Without it, society remains deeply divided. In Bangladesh, it is essential to ensure justice and accountability for crimes committed during the Liberation War, violence in the hill tracts and the July mass uprising. Reconciliation is equally necessary.

These issues emerged in discussions at a session titled ‘Justice, Accountability and National Reconciliation’ at the Bay of Bengal Conversation 2026, organised by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS).

The session was held at a hotel in the capital on Monday. It was the final day of the three-day event.

Teachers and researchers from Bangladesh, South Africa, Cambodia, India and Nepal spoke at the session about the need for justice, accountability and reconciliation.

However, Bangladesh’s Deputy Speaker of Parliament Kayser Kamal, who took part in the session as a panelist, said reconciliation efforts around the world had often failed because they were used as a political shield to protect those involved in state violence from legal consequences.

“National reconciliation without justice is not peace; it is merely a temporary pause in conflict,” he stated.

Citing a United Nations report, Kayser Kamal said as many as 1,600 people had lost their lives during the July mass uprising, with children accounting for 12 to 13 per cent of the deaths.

“This fearless and uncompromising generation fought to build a new country where every citizen would enjoy equal rights and perpetrators would be brought to justice,” he said.

It is worth noting that the UN fact-finding team estimated that as many as 1,400 people may have been killed during the July mass uprising up to 5 August 2024. The government’s list, meanwhile, puts the number of martyrs at 843. No new applications have been received.

Kayser Kamal said everyone was aware that “evil forces” were now desperately trying to regain their political relevance through acts of violence. “Unfortunately, some groups at home and abroad are speaking on their behalf in the name of reconciliation,” he said. “Such thinking will push the country towards a new conflict, the consequences of which could be extremely grave and unimaginable.”

“I want to state this in the clearest and most unequivocal terms: there is no scope for reconciliation with the ousted Awami League (whose activities have been banned in the country),” he said.

The session was moderated by Pramod Jaiswal, research director at the Nepal Institute for International Cooperation and Engagement. He said justice was necessary, but without reconciliation, society could remain deeply divided.

According to Jaiswal, accountability must be clearly distinguished from retribution. In most South Asian societies, he said, accountability was often conflated with revenge.

He said that reconciliation does not mean reaching complete agreement about the past. Nor does it mean forgetting or forgiving serious wrongs or crimes. Rather, it means creating an environment in which individuals and communities can coexist with dignity, acknowledge historical grievances and rebuild trust in one another within state institutions.

Professor Karori Singh of the University of Rajasthan said people entrusted with institutional responsibilities tended to become authoritarian. Against the backdrop of South Asia, he said, such authoritarianism was creating problems in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal.

Madalitso Zililo Phiri, a researcher at the University of the Witwatersrand in South Africa, said the country’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission had been a prerequisite for imagining a new society. The commission had faced considerable criticism, he said, because liberal institutions and democratic arrangements had failed to fulfil all their promises of equality.

Nikki Singer, executive director of Cambodia’s Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies, said Cambodia had suffered a civil war and that reconciliation efforts had begun even before 1991.

Under a national reconciliation process, Khmer Rouge rebel fighters were reintegrated into mainstream society and disarmed in 1998, she said.

Singer said many Cambodians held a personal belief that they could not move forward if they focused solely on blaming people for the past. They also considered what kind of future and legacy they wanted to leave for their children and grandchildren.

Another speaker at the session was Nurul Kabir, president of the Editors Guild and editor of New Age. He said those responsible for crimes in 1971 were still not prepared to acknowledge their wrongdoing. Instead, they continued to seek to justify their actions against humanity.

There is also the problem of the Chittagong Hill Tracts. We can still see hardline nationalist positions among the parties involved in the conflict, he said.

“Similarly, there has been no sign of remorse from those who killed pro-democracy protesters in 2024. They are still accusing the protesters of being extremists and radicals,” he said.

These problems must certainly be resolved, Nurul Kabir said. To make that possible, the parties concerned must be persuaded to acknowledge that they had made mistakes.

He believed this would one day be possible. “Only then can we begin a new journey towards building a society founded on equality, social justice and human dignity,” he said.

item.title: How much longer will we have to wait for media freedom?
item.description:
I would like to begin by recalling an event from sixty-four years ago. On 1 February 1962, the first student strike and protest movement against the military rule of Pakistan took place at the University of Dhaka. Among the many demands raised that day was a very simple but fundamental demand: we must have the right to speak. We must have freedom of the press. I was one of the participants in that protest and strike.

After that, through years of struggle and sacrifice, Bangladesh achieved independence. Over the past fifty-five years, the country has experienced many ups and downs. Governments have changed, political leaders have changed, and the political landscape has changed.

In July-August 2024, a nationwide mass uprising brought down an authoritarian ruler and the system that had been entrenched in the country. The ruler fled the country. It was an extraordinary and almost unbelievable moment in our history.

Then the interim government ran the country for nearly 18 months. People had high expectations from that government. But in many respects, those expectations were not fulfilled. As a result, the current government also continues to bear the mark of failure in managing and running the state. There were initiatives towards political and constitutional reform, but many did not progress very far. Some important recommendations of the reform commissions were also not implemented.

Prothom Alo will remain firm in independent journalism

During the interim government, newspapers, television channels and other media outlets faced considerable difficulties in operating freely. Under various forms of pressure and fear, managements changed, editors were replaced, and many journalists were forced to leave their jobs.

The media industry became increasingly unstable. Some media owners sought relationships with influential people of the new government and placed their followers in positions of responsibility. As a result, newspapers and other media outlets often had to operate in an atmosphere of uncertainty and self-censorship.

Speaking from the experience of Prothom Alo, I can say that we too went through an atmosphere of fear. Throughout that period, we faced pressure and threats from extremist groups. Hateful propaganda was carried out against The Daily Star and Prothom Alo, both inside the country and from abroad. Various groups, both within and outside the government, engaged in multifarious activities. They sought to create instability in the country to achieve their political objectives.

In November 2024, extremists demonstrated in front of the Prothom Alo office for nearly seven days. These activities ultimately culminated in the burning and destruction of Prothom Alo office.

On 18 December 2025, the Prothom Alo office remained on fire for almost the entire night. There was looting and extensive destruction of property. Only after everything had been burned down and destroyed did the law enforcement agencies clear the way for the fire brigade to arrive. Those responsible within the government did not give any direct or effective instructions to the police, RAB or members of the armed forces to prevent the destruction. One or two advisers tried to intervene in their individual capacities, but those efforts were not successful.

By the time dawn broke, the fire and destruction at the Prothom Alo office had ended. Following Prothom Alo, the Daily Star office was also blockaded and set on fire. Its employees were eventually brought out under extremely difficult and suffocating circumstances.

We remember that former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in parliament described Prothom Alo as an enemy of the Awami League, enemy of democracy, and enemy of the country. The editor and journalists of Prothom Alo were also barred from entering the Prime Minister’s Office and from attending various national events. Since her defeat in the 2001 election and after 2009, whenever I met Sheikh Hasina, she did not stop at making hateful remarks; she also used aggressive language.

Although the interim government made various encouraging statements, there was no significant change in the actual situation of the media. The interim government did, however, establish a Media Reform Commission. The commission worked extensively on urgent and important issues concerning the media and proposed a range of short- and long-term measures. There was broad and positive consensus among journalists, editors and media managers on many of these proposals. Unfortunately, the interim government took virtually no initiative to implement them.

After all these experiences, a fair general election was held on 12 February 2026. The government, armed forces, police and administration worked together to conduct a fair election. In that election, BNP secured a major victory and, after nearly nineteen years, returned to power.

The most important question before us now is: what direction will Bangladesh take after this change? And, more specifically: how will we ensure freedom of the media, the safety of journalists, and an environment in which an independent and responsible press can operate freely?

During BNP’s two previous terms in government, from 1991 to 1996 and from 2001 to 2006, I was the editor of Bhorer Kagoj and then Prothom Alo, respectively. During both periods, under BNP governments led by Begum Khaleda Zia, we enjoyed considerable freedom in practising journalism.

In particular, during the 2001–2006 government, we strongly criticised many of its policies and actions. Yet this did not prevent us from having access to the Prime Minister or other leaders. We were not subjected to major harassment or legal action simply because of our criticism.

I remember having heated arguments with Begum Khaleda Zia when she was Prime Minister. At times, both of us became quite agitated during our conversations. But I never had to face punishment for expressing my views. During that period, I also had disagreements and arguments with Tarique Rahman, then a young BNP leader and now the Prime Minister. There were debates between us in the pages of the newspaper as well. Those disagreements were ultimately resolved.

In contrast, during the previous authoritarian government, Prothom Alo and I personally faced grudge from the former prime minister. Institutionally also, we had to live under constant fear. The scope for an independent media was extremely shrunken during the rule of Sheikh Hasina. Journalists and editors faced cases and many were imprisoned.

During that authoritarian rule, various efforts were made to reduce the circulation of Prothom Alo. Government advertisements were withdrawn, and at one point advertisements from around fifty major domestic and international companies were also stopped in August 2015. We remember that in 2000 as well, the Awami League government stopped government advertisements in Prothom Alo and shut down our online edition.

On 30 March 2023, a case was brought against me under the Digital Security Act. At one stage, the number of cases filed against me came close to eighty. Some of those cases are still pending in court.

We remember that former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in parliament described Prothom Alo as an enemy of the Awami League, enemy of democracy, and enemy of the country. The editor and journalists of Prothom Alo were also barred from entering the Prime Minister’s Office and from attending various national events. Since her defeat in the 2001 election and after 2009, whenever I met Sheikh Hasina, she did not stop at making hateful remarks; she also used aggressive language.

The government has completed only seven months of its tenure, and there is still considerable time ahead. Even taking this into consideration, we can say that the urgent issues facing newspapers and the broader media need to be addressed without delay. Otherwise, the freedom and aspirations of journalists and editors in this country could face a crisis. And in such a situation, I repeatedly find myself thinking of that day sixty-four years ago, 1 February 1962. That day, we raised the demand: we must have the right to speak. We must have freedom of the press.

After all that, in early 2024, the military intelligence agency exerted tremendous pressure on the chief executive of our company to give up ownership of Prothom Alo. Behind that pressure was also an effort to remove the editor. There was effort to take ownership of Prothom Alo away and hand it over to a highly discredited and notorious business group involved in money laundering. All of this was done at the direction of Sheikh Hasina.

The situation had reached such a point that, had that government remained in power for a few more months, the management of Prothom Alo could have been taken away from us, and I might no longer have been able to remain its editor. We had to pass through those extremely painful and difficult days. Those experiences have left an indelible scar on our minds.

After the authoritarian Awami League government and the multiple crises experienced during the interim government, the return of BNP to power has created a sense of optimism among the people. Given BNP’s past experience with newspapers and the media, we hope that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and the BNP government will, during this important transitional period, continue to adopt a tolerant and constructive attitude towards newspapers, television and the broader media.

BNP’s commitments concerning the media in its 31-point political programme and election manifesto have strengthened this expectation. In our multiple meetings and candid discussions with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, we have had quite positive discussions about the present and future of newspapers and the media. Point 11 of the BNP’s 31-point reform programme specifically addresses the media. It proposes establishing a Media Commission headed by a Supreme Court judge to ensure full media freedom and comprehensive reform of the sector. It also commits to restoring an environment for honest and independent journalism.

BNP’s election manifesto also outlines several other initiatives under the heading ‘Media’. It states that fearless and impartial journalism will be protected and recognised, and that objective criticism will be welcomed. It says that ensuring the professional independence and security of journalists who engage in constructive and objective criticism is a responsibility of the state. It also proposes legal mechanisms and a special cell to prevent harassment and persecution of journalists.

But despite these commitments by BNP as a political party and by the government, no significant steps have yet been taken to reform the newspaper and broader media sector. The Ministry of Information has expressed interest in introducing a system for auditing newspapers and clearing long-outstanding bills, but these initiatives have yet to be implemented. There was also a meeting to discuss urgent reforms needed in newspapers, television and the wider media sector following the proposal to establish a Media Commission. Since then, however, we have heard little about the matter.

Media reforms and the question of counter revolution

Over the past few months, there have also been reports of unwelcome interference and changes in the internal management of some newspapers and television channels. Some editors and senior journalists are saying that they continue to operate under uncertainty and pressure. In some cases, journalists are exercising self-censorship or excessive caution over particular reports and opinions. There are reports that, in some newspapers, pressure is being exerted over independent journalism and freedom of expression. This is undermining the environment for independent journalism.

Some public or private discussions by senior government figures have also become a cause of concern for us. There are also concerns about the way the government is dealing with the Cyber Security Act and the possibility that journalism and freedom of expression could, under certain circumstances, be placed at risk.

The government has completed only seven months of its tenure, and there is still considerable time ahead. Even taking this into consideration, we can say that the urgent issues facing newspapers and the broader media need to be addressed without delay. Otherwise, the freedom and aspirations of journalists and editors in this country could face a crisis. And in such a situation, I repeatedly find myself thinking of that day sixty-four years ago, 1 February 1962. That day, we raised the demand: we must have the right to speak. We must have freedom of the press.

Over this long period, governments have changed. Political leaders have changed. The political landscape has changed. Yet the fundamental issues behind our demands seem to have remained largely where they were. At the end of my 56-year career in journalism, I find myself standing in the same place once again. Unfortunatly, we still have to speak about those demands. We still have to ask for them. How much longer will we have to wait?

* Matiur Rahman, editor, Prothom Alo

item.title: Humaiun Kobir in keynote address: National interest will be the priority, not any single side
item.description:
Foreign Affairs State Minister Humaiun Kobir has made it clear that Bangladesh will not choose sides amid growing strategic competition among major powers.

He further said national interest would be the guiding principle of Bangladesh’s foreign policy. Rather than relying on any single side, Bangladesh wants to maintain strategic autonomy through cooperation with different countries.

Humaiun Kobir made the remarks in a keynote address on the concluding day of the Bay of Bengal Conversation at a hotel in the capital yesterday, Monday.

The three-day international conference was organised by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS). Yesterday was the final day of the conference.

The state minister said that the world is changing rapidly and the centres of power are shifting, creating both challenges and new opportunities for Bangladesh.

According to him, the competition among major powers in international relations should not be viewed as an opportunity to choose one side over another.

“Our policy is not to take any particular side; our policy is to choose what is best for Bangladesh’s national interests,” he said.

Where interests converge, Bangladesh will cooperate, while differences will be addressed through dialogue and diplomacy, he stated.

Referring to economic diplomacy as a key instrument of foreign policy, the state minister said there is no longer any scope to view foreign policy and economic policy separately.

Bangladesh’s missions abroad need to play a more active role in exploring new markets, attracting investment and promoting Bangladeshi products.

Describing South Asia as one of the least integrated regions in the world, he stressed the need for stronger regional connectivity, trade and energy cooperation.

Speaking on the Rohingya crisis, Humaiun Kobir said Bangladesh has been sheltering more than one million forcibly displaced Rohingya, but humanitarian assistance is not a permanent solution to the crisis.

Describing the issue as a top priority for national security and foreign policy, he said Bangladesh would raise the issue more forcefully on the international multilateral platform when it assumes the presidency of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

He identified the safe, voluntary, dignified and sustainable return of the Rohingya as the ultimate goal.

Identifying cyber, food, energy, water and climate security as non-traditional security challenges, the state minister said cross-border cooperation is essential to address problems that transcend national borders.

Addressing the climate change issue, he said Bangladesh faces serious risks despite making a negligible contribution to global carbon emissions. He therefore highlighted the need for greater climate justice and adaptation financing.

The foreign affairs state minister outlined four core principles of Bangladesh’s foreign policy: national interest will serve as the guiding principle; strategic autonomy will provide strength; partnerships will expand new opportunities; and peace will remain the ultimate goal.

Sheikh Hasina’s activities in India main challenge to PM’s Delhi visit
item.description:
The “principal challenge” in planning Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to India is the activities of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and leaders of her party currently staying there, Foreign Affairs State Minister Humaiun Kobir has said.

He made the remarks in an interview with Indian newspaper The Hindu on Monday.

Responding to questions from The Hindu on the sidelines of the Bay of Bengal Conversation 2026, organised by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS) in Dhaka, Humaiun Kobir said India needed to realise “the challenges facing the newly elected government” in Bangladesh.

He also said the activities of leaders of the Awami League, whose activities are currently banned in the country, while in exile would not be helpful to India.

‘Destabilising another country’

Urging India to restrain Sheikh Hasina and her exiled party leaders, Humaiun Kobir said in the interview that the visit will be bilateral, but there are some challenges, and both sides will overcome them through dialogue.

According to him, Bangladesh was not asking for too much when it comes to the main challenge. “Sheikh Hasina and her team are staying in Delhi and they are trying to destabilise another country from there. This is not helping India either.”

Humaiun Kobir accused Sheikh Hasina of being responsible for the deaths of nearly 2,000 Bangladeshi citizens during the suppression of the July-August 2024 uprising. He described her as “a terrorist”.

He said Bangladeshis needed a “clean break” with their past, as people had sacrificed their lives in the process of ousting Sheikh Hasina’s government, which had remained in power for more than 15 years.

The state minister, however, said that discussions with India were under way and that Dhaka welcomed the dialogue.

Describing relations with India as a priority for Dhaka, Humaiun Kobir told The Hindu, “We are seeing some positive signs as India is trying to restrain them. That is the norm between two countries. If they (Hasina and her team) are restrained, then there will be no problem in the [bilateral] relationship.”

Highlighting the role of Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi in this regard, Humaiun Kobir said, “The visit of the Prime Minister will take place at a conducive time and I am hopeful. The PM has never said that he will not visit [India].”

Indian high commissioner’s role

Describing the Awami League leadership as an “obstacle” to normalising Dhaka-Delhi relations, Humaiun Kobir said, “The Indian High Commissioner here is doing a good role. He is trying and hopefully Delhi will be receptive to his opinion and if they give importance to his opinion, then we are ready to engage across the board. We are carrying out our consultations.”

The state minister said Bangladesh was ready to discuss all issues but expected some “reciprocation”.

Saying that Bangladesh would not allow anyone to operate from Dhaka against India’s interests, Humaiun Kobir said he expected India to take similar measures.

“When two governments sit down to discuss keeping in mind national interests, all issues can be addressed,” he told The Hindu.

The Hindu correspondent is visiting Dhaka as a guest of the Centre for Governance Studies to attend the Bay of Bengal Conversation 2026.

item.title: Applications open for news presenters at BTV for both Bengali and English
item.description:
A great opportunity has emerged to present news on Bangladesh Television (BTV), one of the country’s oldest, most established and prestigious media institutions.

For those who have long dreamed of building a career in television through fluent delivery, clear pronunciation and confident presentation, this is an excellent opportunity.

Bangladesh Television has invited applications from interested and eligible candidates to present news in both Bengali and English.

Joining the state-owned broadcaster as a news presenter is not only a professional achievement but also a position of considerable responsibility and prestige, involving the delivery of reliable information to millions of people across the country.

Applicants must submit their applications by 7 October 2026. As only a few days remain before the deadline, interested candidates are advised to prepare their applications promptly and send them to the designated address.

Candidates can submit their applications through several convenient channels, allowing applicants from across the country to apply easily. Those wishing to apply in person or by post can send their applications by courier or post to the designated address:

Deputy Director-General (News), Bangladesh Television, Headquarters Building, Rampura, Dhaka-1219.

In line with modern digital communication, applicants can also submit their applications electronically. They can send their CV with a photograph and application through the official email address (newsaudition@btv.gov.bd) or via WhatsApp at 01332125138.

Bangladesh Television’s news presenter selection process is highly competitive and transparent.

The opportunity is particularly suitable for those with strong language and pronunciation skills, an individual style of news presentation, and the ability to present contemporary issues fluently.

For young and experienced media professionals who aspire to appear on BTV and begin a new chapter in their media careers through news presentation, this opportunity is highly significant.

Submit your application with a complete CV to the designated address or through the digital channels and take the opportunity to work with Bangladesh Television.

item.title: ‘I paid for my uniform with bribes to take bribes’
item.description:
A video circulating on social media shows Mohammad Elias Hossain, an assistant sub-inspector (ASI) of Chunarughat Police Station in Habiganj, saying, “I paid for my uniform with bribes so that I could take bribes.”

Elias Hossain reportedly made the remarks while visiting Ranigaon Bazar in Chunarughat upazila as part of an investigation into a case. A local resident recorded his remarks on a mobile phone. The video later spread on social media, drawing criticism.

In the video, ASI Elias Hossain is heard saying, “People say things only after seeing something happen, don’t they? Don’t you understand? If I say I’m a police officer and I don’t take bribes, I am the imam of Baitul Mukarram would it be believable? I paid for my uniform with bribes, so that I could take bribes.”

According to local sources, ASI Elias Hossain had gone to Ranigaon Bazar to investigate a case filed by Noman Mia, a businessman there. He made the remarks in front of people who were present at the time.

Meanwhile, several local residents have alleged that ASI Elias Hossain has demanded bribes while investigating various cases. They claimed that he shows little interest in investigating cases unless he is paid a bribe.

Allegations of irregularities had also emerged against Elias Hossain while he was investigating a case filed over allegations of child abuse and attempted rape in Tekarghat village of Gazipur Union in the upazila. The allegation is that he took financial benefits from the defendants and pressured and intimidated the complainant to withdraw the case.

Local residents have also alleged that Elias Hossain exercises influence at the police station and in investigations by identifying Officer-in-Charge (OC) Saiful Islam of Chunarughat Police Station as his “big brother” in the area. However, the allegation could not be independently verified.

When contacted about the video, ASI Mohammad Elias Hossain said, “I don’t know anything about this.” He then disconnected the phone.

When contacted by phone, Chunarughat Police Station OC Saiful Islam said, “I have seen the video. It is being verified. I will sit down with him [ASI Elias Hossain] to try to find out the context in which he made the remarks.”

item.title: Dengue cases surge in Chittagong, 21 deaths recorded this year
item.description:
The dengue outbreak in Chittagong is intensifying, with 4,914 infections and 21 deaths recorded in the district between January 1 and October 5.
The situation worsened sharply in September, when 2,430 cases and 16 deaths were reported.
According to the District Civil Surgeon’s Office, 107 new dengue cases were detected in the 24 hours until 8am on Sunday. Of the 4,914 patients recorded this year, 260 are currently undergoing treatment at different hospitals, while 4,654 have recovered and been discharged.
The dengue situation remained relatively mild at the beginning of the year, with 68 cases in January, 22 in February, 20 in March, 29 in April and 37 in May.
Cases began rising in June, reaching 122 that month, followed by 536 in July and 1,202 in August. The number surged to 2,430 in September.
Another 448 cases were reported in the first five days of October.
September was also the deadliest month, accounting for 16 of the 21 deaths recorded this year. Two deaths each were reported in July and August, while one was recorded in February.
No new dengue deaths were reported in the 24 hours preceding the latest update.
According to data from the District Civil Surgeon’s Office, 2,285 of the 4,914 cases were reported in Chittagong city, 2,098 in different upazilas and 531 among patients who came from other districts.
Among the upazilas, Sitakunda recorded the highest number of cases at 620, followed by Karnaphuli with 285, Banshkhali 154, Rangunia 152, Satkania 121, Anwara 112, Raozan 103 and Patiya 100.
Other cases were reported in Hathazari (84), Chandanaish (77), Boalkhali (76), Mirsharai (79), Lohagara (66), Fatikchhari (44) and Sandwip (25).
Of the total dengue patients recorded this year, 2,402 are men, 1,403 are women and 1,109 are children.
Among the 107 patients admitted in the 24-hour period, 56 were men, 23 were women and 28 were children.
However, women accounted for the highest number of deaths. Of the 21 people who died, 11 were women, six were children and four were men.
The number of dengue cases recorded in Chittagong this year has already surpassed the totals for the previous two years.
The district recorded 4,323 cases and 45 deaths in 2024, while 4,864 cases and 27 deaths were reported in 2025.
As of October 5 this year, the number of cases stood at 4,914, with 21 deaths.
Residents have complained that mosquito-control activities in Chittagong have not kept pace with the rising number of dengue cases.
Muntasir Uddin, a resident of Sangeet Residential Area in Hamzarbag, said mosquito infestations in the area had become severe, while City Corporation workers assigned to mosquito control were rarely seen.
He also alleged a lack of supervision over the effectiveness of insecticide spraying.
Jamal Uddin, a resident of Chandanpura, said the number of dengue patients in the city had increased significantly, but City Corporation monitoring had not increased proportionately.
District Civil Surgeon Mohammad Sajedur Rahman told Bangla Tribune that dengue is a mosquito-borne disease and urged residents to keep their surroundings clean.
He said dengue could be controlled by destroying mosquito breeding grounds and advised people to undergo dengue tests and seek medical advice promptly if they develop a fever.
Sheikh Fazle Rabbi, divisional director of health in Chittagong, also advised people to consult a doctor immediately if they develop fever or symptoms of dengue.
He said the most important measure to prevent dengue was to destroy Aedes mosquito breeding grounds, while efforts should also be made to eliminate adult mosquitoes.
He said the City Corporation had been sent several letters urging it to intensify mosquito-control activities.
Ashraful Amin, chief executive officer and secretary of Chittagong City Corporation, told Bangla Tribune that the corporation was conducting regular mosquito-control activities to combat dengue and other mosquito-borne diseases.
He said special “crash programmes” were also being conducted in different areas when necessary.
Amin said dengue could not be controlled through insecticide spraying alone and stressed the need to destroy mosquito breeding grounds.
He also urged residents to prevent water from stagnating in and around their homes, rooftops, construction sites and other areas.

item.title: Dhaka ranks first globally in air pollution
item.description:
Dhaka ranked first among the world's most polluted cities on Tuesday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 213 at 11:10am.
The air quality was classified as "very unhealthy", signalling a serious health alert where everyone may experience health effects, according to the AQI scale.
Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia ranked second with an AQI score of 208, while Singapore in Singapore ranked third with a score of 179 and Kolkata in India ranked fourth with an AQI score of 177.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while 151 to 200 is classified as "unhealthy". A reading between 201 and 300 is considered "very unhealthy", while levels above 301 are deemed "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Hair is political
item.description:
When I was six, I contracted a severe case of typhoid. I had to get injections for ten days straight.
My relatives recommended that I shave my hair off. I would be willing to shave my hair for the right cause today without hesitation, just like my favorite fashion designer, Vivienne Westwood.
She shaved her hair to raise awareness for climate change. But this was too terrifying for my six-year-old self. I had grown my hair out for a while, and I was afraid to let it all go.
Furthermore, I was too sick to even understand what was going on with me. I only remember sitting on the balcony under the sun with my Naan while she carefully brushed my hair and ran a razor over my head.
That was the first time I remembered how my face looked without hair. I was quickly taught the realities of society that hair is everything, especially if you are a woman.
One of my favorite scenes from Fleabag is when her sister gets a bad haircut in a moment of weakness, and she reframes it by saying, “Claire, it's French," because the worst thing you can do as a woman is not look palatable and resist the patriarchal male gaze.
To become the worst thing this society has encountered is to be an angry feminist who doesn’t shave her body hair or cuts her hair too short.
Hair is political, be it for Black women who had to fight to be taken seriously in their Afro hair or Chinese women who dye their hair pink right before graduation to honor Zheng Linghua, who committed suicide because she was cyberbullied for her hair color.
In a world where Iranian woman Mahsa Amini is beaten to death because her hair was not properly covered, it is equally political if you are a South Asian or Bengali woman raised in a conservative Muslim household.
I grew up in a small, secluded area in Puran Dhaka called Hazaribagh. Boys played cricket and rode bicycles, filling my neighborhood. Meanwhile, little girls enjoyed playing Kanamachhi and Ekka-Dokka.
I was a restless, clumsy, boyish child whom the boys made fun of because I wanted to play with them.
When I was about four years old, I stole my brother’s shirt, wore it, and ran away from my house. I assumed I was indistinguishable from boys my age which could not be further from the truth.
I was a rebellious child with a bowl cut who wanted to play cricket with boys and ruin my clothes with dust.
People around me didn’t quite like it. My parents were desperate to find a school that was as diligent about grades and cultural activities as it was strict about instilling manners.
They found the school they wanted. With its merits, this school also instilled in me a fear of judgment.
My mother used to make two ponytails when I had short hair; it was the dress code. I never questioned it. I did not have long hair until I was in third grade.
When my hair grew longer, different rules started to apply to me. Now, it was mandatory for me to make two braids. I still did not question it.
Every morning, my mother would braid my hair. Meanwhile, my father ironed his shirt, humming "Amar Sara Deho Kheo Mati" by Andrew Kishore.
As I never questioned the decision of making two mandatory pigtails, I never suffered the consequence of breaking the dress code.
Until my mother received a diagnosis of a chronic illness at the end of my fourth grade, I had nobody to braid my hair.
I brushed my hair in a disheveled manner and made one big ponytail. My father dropped me at school. For the first time, I was about to break the rule.
So long, I had only seen what happened to the girls who didn’t brush their hair according to the rules.
Sometimes, if you were lucky, you were only yelled at.
If your class teacher was strict, you got threats of having your hair chopped off.
If your luck was terrible, you might get slut-shamed for your hairstyle. This would happen even if you were in grade four.
Accusing you of luring men at an all-girls school is both unfair and ridiculous. You only wanted to style your hair differently.
After fifth grade, I switched to a different school. It was a combined school where boys would study in the day shift and girls in the morning. I was hoping things would be different here.
To my disappointment, your hair still dictated your reputation. Breaking the rule of two mandatory pigtails was equivalent to wearing the Scarlet Letter.
We were taught to treat people like they were aliens or as if they were a different species just on the basis of our assigned genders at birth. Segregated schools made it worse.
It’s as if we are peeking at the zoo animals when one shift ends and another one starts.
It didn’t help that most of our teachers were head-to-toe misogynistic; some of them were women. Male teachers and female teachers showcased different cases of misogyny. Male teachers displayed either benevolent misogyny or inappropriate behavior.
Benevolent misogyny meant they believed women needed protection, so they wouldn’t hit female students but felt free to abuse boys.
Inappropriate behavior included flirting that bordered on harassment and even attempted grooming.
From female teachers, the accusations felt more guttural and personal. It typically began with thinly veiled concerns and concluded with slutshaming.
Despite society's constant pressure on girls to meet beauty standards, they still face shame for their hairstyles and their desire to look ornate.
There was a strong association in the minds of these women that these school girls only wanted to doll up, wear their ponytails instead of two braids, and plump their lips with fruity chapsticks to entice the boys from the day shift.
They would try to warn us by telling us that we should be independent instead of chasing a man, but their heteronormative assumptions that only a boy can be the object of desire in a girl’s world, suggesting that this is the sole focus for teenage girls, reinforce harmful stereotypes and promote heteronormative behavior.
This type of social indoctrination is what keeps so many women in shackles of compulsory heterosexuality.
Today, I am in university, and I have the freedom to cut, dye, and wear my hair however I want.
To this day, I still cannot find the answer to a question.
How is your hair a testament to your character?
Asmita Mehefin likes to look at the moon and write poems and compare how the celestial bodies are similar to the web of life inside our own bodies.

item.title: The Strange Grief of Turning 18
item.description:
To me this birthday was not special because I turned 18; sadly, the breeze of responsibility and the fear of adulthood have not crept into my life yet. However, the reason this birthday lingered within me for quite long is because this was that day when I actually felt the time flying.
If I am to leave for my universities abroad next year, this would be my last September in Dhaka.
Last September, October, and all the last. In fact, maybe the last birthday that I ever get to celebrate in my own home with my own people.
For the last two or three years, I had this tradition I followed. I bought cake from my favorite bakery and cut the cake the night before my birthday.
There was always something about waking up the morning of your birthday and having the leftover cake from midnight.
This time though, I could not really stick to that.
I returned from my coaching classes, and my sister came home from her university classes a lot later and jumped straight to her online meetings. Maybe I was physically drained out from fatigue or just mentally drained out; I could not even stay awake till 12.
My body was giving up, and I did not want it to get consumed with all the birthday depression, reflections, and everything. But well, I think I failed at that; here we are talking about life again.
I woke up in the morning, put on the dress I had chosen in my mind, and got a birthday photoshoot done, this time with flowers.
I never bought flower bouquets on my birthday, but for this last time I thought I would.
On my way back from tuition in Dhanmondi, right beside the bakery was that flower shop I always wanted to buy flowers from.
And the occasion could not have been more perfect.
Something so memorable about this birthday would be that on my way back with the flowers and cake, when I was on a rickshaw ride home, I saw a star.
Yes, for the first time in these 18 years of life, I saw a star for the first time. That genuinely felt different; maybe it was a way of the universe greeting me, patting me on my back for coming this far.
After the cake-cutting ceremony with family was over, I was back at the desk, finally opening my social media to see the wishes. I already knew that one friend who would go the extra mile to write such a loving paragraph and greet me at 12 and then end up getting worried about me not responding in time.
Then came all the other wishes of people who have been such important parts of my life at times and still continue to be.
This one day of the year, and also the results day, I see my DMs flooded. It feels lively to see how much you are cared for, but yet so ungrateful.
Then as the day slowly passed, the feeling crept in, the weight of emotions, flashbacks of life, of how grateful I am to God for making me survive all these years of life despite everything.
Well, at the end of the day things do get better, and for every bad thing that happens in life, I get something good in return—a lot better, I would say. And that is when I realize, if I had given up back then, I would not be able to cherish the joys life had offered to me eventually.
I never really understood why some people cry on their birthdays, but now I do.
Suddenly then, a notification from Google Photos pops up: 10 years ago.
And within a while, I have scrolled down to all the previous birthdays till now. Seeing the familiar faces of families, of relatives, of friends, of myself, even how I had grown up. It was almost like a film rolled on, a walk down the memory lane.
I made a vlog with my family of all the five of us cutting the cake together, and I know I will cry the next time I rewatch this video when I am 25 or something (God, I hope I make it till then). I wanted this birthday to feel perfect, to be everything I wanted for one last time, and to me it was.
I would not, however, say that it was something I could make a documentary on, maybe because it was real; it reminded me of everything one last time, of how life with time would eventually change and you would have no control over it.
Labiba Tasnim is currently studying in 12th grade at S.F.X. Greenherald International School.
